author: ValWood
body: OK found it. All of these appear to come from a single mouse paper PMID:27374330 and are all IMPs? Look at all the annotations this has spawned from multiple sources! ~Panther, Ensemlb IEA, ARBA manual ISO???!!! This isn't just an ARBA problem, it's a general propagation problem. @cmungall @hattrill a good example. This isn't an ARBA issue, in fact ARBA mostly identifies the problems in the underlying annotation~ I don't completely know the biology here, but in yeast cps1 is THE main resident vacuolar carboxypeptidase. It is used a lot as an assay to identify secretory because in any secretory pathway mutant, it is missorted to the cell surface. I wouldn't imagine it is doing very much differently in higher eukaryotes. Are there any later papers? Antoinia, maybe it would be good to tighten up the rules for Funfams so that it only applies the very lax rule to MF annotations and not to BP. https://www.alliancegenome.org/gene/HGNC:26518#function---go-annotations vw: edited, the other annotations are OK, although I wouldn't annotate this paper to amino acid or lipid metabolism...

author: ValWood
body:
> Of course, the human/mouse ortholog might be functionally diverged from the yeast, but that would be unusual.

I can't find any evidence that in yeast carboxypeptidase Y has specificity for anything other than peptide bonds or amides (but peptide bonds are a class of amide bonds)

but the "amide catabolic process" is a strange grouping term (because it's a type of bond, not  really a process). it would be better to capture activity here  because  this  process could mean anything, see the children:
https://www.ebi.ac.uk/QuickGO/term/GO:0043605

At least it only has 11 EXP annotation => suggest obsoletion, unnecessary grouping term.

The term is also problematic because peptides and proteins are amides, but they aren't related (resulting in a lot of missing subclasses). I will open a ticket to obsolete  "amide metabolic/biosynthetic/catabolic process"

author: ValWood
body:
It might be more useful to build up a list of the most common failure modes.

This one would be  "transferring between kingdoms based on 2 metazoan annotations to a FUNFAM family/ neofunctionalization in human"    

@Antonialock The Pombe family has only a single member, so I assumed it was a 1:1 mapping; however, does this FUNFAM have more members in humans? And if so, does this annotation also get transferred to those?

The FUNFAMs are usually confined to orthologous groups, but it might work if the rule could be expanded so that processes are not transferred for multi-member families.
I think this one would be tricky for ANY method based on orthology  because of the neofunctionalization.
The other thing I don't yet undersatnd is- this annotation does not get transferred to budding yeast based on the conflict with its existing annotation so why transfer to other fungi?

@Antonialock  could we get a list of all the ARBA rules?
(not the individual rules, but the subtly differnrt allowed rule structures for specific types of family- like the fact that only 2 annotations are required for RFAM).
This would be very helpful.

author: ValWood
body:
This is  odd. cps1 and PM20D1 are clearly reciprocal best hits

~https://www.flyrnai.org/cgi-bin/DRSC_orthologs.pl?input_species=4896&output_species=0&additional_filter=None&search_fields=***&search_datasets=***&gene_list=SPAC24C9.08
I wonder if the PM20D1 gene has truly lost its ancestral function.
I can't find any papers that look at the cellular location. Only that it is "secreted", but so is cps1 in some circumstances. 
I wonder if PM20D1  also localises to the lysosome (functionally)- it seems to be expressed in lots of cell types (neurones, cardiomyocytes) . Perhaps this is a specialised cell type-specific activity.
 I couldn't find any actual cellular localisation data for this protein (human or mouse), other than its detection in the lysate and conditional media.~

actually the conservation is a bit inconsistent between eukaryotes, not always 1:1

author: Antonialock
body:
I think the developers use the term "negating annotations" in a different way from how we would use it. I think they use it to mean that we are adding more data that can be used to train the model, so the constraints for a rule will change ("negating the annotation" = the annotation won't be valid any longer. So here, with adding that TAS, you just added a "negative" example)

for GO, ARBA can learn on these evidence codes:
Inferred from Experiment (EXP)
Inferred from Direct Assay (IDA)
Inferred from Physical Interaction (IPI)
Inferred from Mutant Phenotype (IMP)
Inferred from Genetic Interaction (IGI)
Inferred from Expression Pattern (IEP)
Traceable Author Statement (TAS)
Inferred by Curator (IC)

author: ValWood
body:
> So here, with adding that TAS, you just added a "negative" example)

but it isn't a negative example, because annotations can co-occur?

author: Antonialock
body:
yes, it is not how we curators would use "negative example".

because you have added a TAS to "protein catabolic process in the vacuole" but not any of those other terms e.g. adaptive thermogenesis, ARBA will take this into consideration when making constraints on the rules that propagate e.g. "adaptive thermogenesis" to entries in funfams 3.40.630.10:FF:000027 + 1.10.150.900:FF:000003 (ARBA00089174, one of the examples). 

I am hoping that ARBA will restrict the term to e.g, mammals, but for all the tickets "I'm hoping will be fixed" I will check back to see what actually happened. It will definitely disappear for pombe, but I don't have an understanding of how the taxon constraints will be recalculated.
